UNESCO Digital Learning Week 2026: Education in the age of AI

From 8 to 11 September, UNESCO brought together in Paris over 25 ministers of education, high-level experts, representatives of the tech industry, and educators and students from around the world to discuss the latest developments and perspectives in the field of artificial intelligence (AI) and education. The event was marked by the adoption, on 8 September, of a joint Ministerial statement calling for education to be sustained as a human right and a common good in the age of AI.
Read more

Prepare the world for AI,
Prepare AI for the world

Today, in an era shaped by Artificial Intelligence (AI) and related breakthrough innovations, UNESCO continues the critical work of ensuring these emerging technologies are developed and deployed in service of equity, opportunity, and inclusivity, for the people.

Coordinated by UNESCO and the ITU as the joint UN Secretariat, the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance (6–7 July)—mandated by the General Assembly—aims to ensure that AI governance reflects the priorities of all nations, not just the most technologically advanced.

World Heritage Committee Gathers to Protect Humanity's Legacy

From 19 to 29 July 2026, the Republic of Korea hosts the 48th session of UNESCO's World Heritage Committee in Busan. Members of the 21-member World Heritage Committee, elected from among the 196 countries, exercise a central responsibility under the World Heritage Convention by determining which new sites to inscribe to the World Heritage List and monitoring the conservation of already listed sites.

Heritage and innovation make Beijing World Capital of Architecture 2029

The capital of the People's Republic of China has been designated as the UNESCO–UIA (International Union of Architects) World Capital of Architecture 2029 by the Director-General of UNESCO, Khaled El-Enany.

The designation was made upon the recommendation of the Joint Committee for the World Capital of Architecture, chaired by the distinguished architect, Dominique Perrault.

Delivering for people in crisis

Culture, education, science, and information are essential needs in times of turbulence and crisis. They are powerful drivers of social cohesion, resilience, and hope in a better future.

UNESCO plays a vital role in safeguarding the social and cultural foundations that underpin stability, dignity, and recovery for communities affected by crises. By protecting these pillars, we help ensure that societies can rebuild not only infrastructure, but also trust, identity, and the collective capacity to move forward.

UNESCO in brief

UNESCO is the United Nations organization that promotes cooperation in education, science, culture and communication to foster peace worldwide.

The Organization provides key services for its Member States, setting global norms and standards, developing tools for international cooperation, producing knowledge for public policies and building global networks of sites and institutions inscribed on its lists.

Is journalism old news?

At a time when anyone can publish and share content, an abundance of information guarantees neither its quality nor its accuracy. 

While digital platforms amplify access to the public arena as well as to information, they can also undermine the conditions for independent journalism. 

In this disrupted landscape, a critical question arises: how can we preserve journalism that is based on verified facts, sound judgment, and the public interest?

UNESCO, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, is a specialized agency dedicated to strengthening international cooperation in the fields of education, science, culture, and information.

We set standards, produce tools and develop knowledge to create solutions to some of the greatest challenges of our time, and foster a world of greater equality and peace.

Protecting biodiversity, responding to artificial intelligence, advancing quality education, safeguarding heritage, and ensuring access to reliable information are some examples of the work that UNESCO does with its 194 Member States across the globe.

UNESCO’s core functions turn discussions among decision-makers into tangible benefits for people. International ideas become policies, programmes and local actions that improve everyday life.

UNESCO Constitution

"Peace based exclusively upon the political and economic arrangements of governments would not be a peace which could secure the unanimous, lasting and sincere support of the peoples of the world, [...] peace must therefore be founded, if it is not to fail, upon the intellectual and moral solidarity of mankind."

UNESCO governance

UNESCO is led by three key bodies: the General Conference, the Secretariat and the Executive Board.

The General Conference, with representatives from all Member States, determines UNESCO's main lines of work. The Secretariat executes the Organization's programme under the authority of the Director-General. The Executive Board monitors the implementation of the Organization's programme.  

Together, these bodies drive UNESCO’s efforts in education, science, culture, and communication.

Transforming lives through education

We promote quality education and lifelong learning for all to build a better future.

Furthering science for sustainability

We support scientific cooperation to enhance sustainability and support public policies.

Building fairer and inclusive societies

We strengthen social policies and advocate for emerging technologies to benefit all.

Protecting our heritage and fostering creativity

We promote and safeguard culture to build resilient communities.

Promoting freedom of expression and access to quality information

We support information literacy, protection of journalists and stronger digital governance.

Protecting the health of our shared ocean for future generations

We foster international cooperation in marine sciences to improve ocean management.

Supporting Africa's development

Through Priority Africa, we emphasize education, culture, and innovation to empower African societies and foster resilience.

Empowering through equality

Through Priority Gender Equality, we aim to empower both women and men through education, inclusion, and equal opportunities.

We set standards, produce tools and develop knowledge to create solutions to some of the greatest challenges of our time, and foster a world of greater equality and peace. General History of Africa: UNESCO opens exhibition on its landmark editorial project

UNESCO invites you to the opening of the ‘Heritages and Contributions of Africa to the Progress of Humanity’ exhibition, which will be displayed at UNESCO Headquarters in Paris from 17 to 22 September 2026. Drawing on the Organization’s landmark General History of Africa series, the exhibit will highlight the contributions of the continent and its diasporas to our shared history, as well as the role of knowledge and memory in building a Culture of Peace in Africa.
UNESCO
11 September 2026
  • What? Inauguration of the exhibition ‘Heritages and Contributions of Africa to the Progress of Humanity’
  • When? Thursday 17 September 2026, 6:00 p.m. (Doors open at 5:45 p.m.)
  • Where? UNESCO Headquarters, 7 Place de Fontenoy, Paris
  • Accreditation: Please register here

The opening ceremony will include opening remarks by:

Mr Khaled El-Enany, Director-General of UNESCO;

H.E. the Ambassador and Permanent Delegate of Angola to UNESCO, representing the host country and co-organizer of the Biennale of Luanda;

H.E. the Ambassador and Permanent Delegate of Senegal to UNESCO, in his capacity as Chairperson of the Africa Group at UNESCO.

These opening remarks will be followed by the official opening of the exhibition and an informal tour led by historian Amzat Boukari-Yabara, curator of the exhibition and contributor to the latest volume of the General History of Africa, in the presence of African Permanent Delegations and UNESCO representatives.

Through a historical and Pan-African journey, the exhibition highlights the contributions of Africa and its diasporas to the history and progress of humanity. At the heart of the exhibition is the General History of Africa, one of UNESCO’s major scientific projects. With the recent publication of Volumes IX, X and XI, the General History of Africa continues its ambition to redefine our understanding of African history from African perspectives, while also making this knowledge available to new generations. The exhibition also highlights how a deeper understanding of history helps to building and foster of a culture of peace and non-violence.

Through archival documents, photographs, maps, publications, iconography and audiovisual resources, visitors will explore topics including: Timbuktu and its scientific traditions, the civilizations of Aksum and Great Zimbabwe, the Haitian Revolution, Pan-African movements, African independence movements and the struggle against apartheid.

This initiative also represents an important milestone ahead of the 4th edition of the Biennale of Luanda – Pan-African Forum for the Culture of Peace and Non-Violence, which will take place in Angola on 22 and 23 October 2026. The exhibition itself was conceived as part of this broader momentum.

The exhibition will be open to the public at UNESCO Headquarters in Paris from 17 to 22 September 2026.

Iraqi CSOs Respond to Surge in Harmful Online Content with Coordinated Monitoring Initiative

28 April 2026
UNESCO
11 September 2026

Since the escalation of the regional war involving Iran in late February, Iraq’s digital information environment has experienced a significant surge in harmful online narratives, hate speech, disinformation campaigns, and targeted harassment across social media platforms. As soon as the conflict started, media actors, academics and CSOs quickly mobilized to set up a team to monitor the situation online, paying special attention to the trends in disinformation, hate speech, and threats and attacks against journalists.

These organizations leading the monitoring of social media, are part of the coalition of organizations that UNESCO has been supporting and equipping with key competencies on Freedom of Expression, disinformation and hate speech online as part of the Social Media 4 Peace Project. This initiative, which is supported by the European Union is working with national stakeholders in Iraq to strengthen the resilience to online harms while protecting freedom of expression and access to information. 

Five organizations from the coalition of CSOs took the lead in the monitoring of content online during this period of crisis to decipher what is driving online harmful content, what patterns can be identified, and what recommendations can be made. These organisations include: ANAT for Media Development, Iraqi Digital Reporting Platform for Female Journalists, Journalists Home (KRI), Iraqi Centre for Strategic Analytics, and Media Monitoring Centre. In less than a month, from 5 to 29 March 2026, the team monitored thousands of posts in social media, and closely studied and analysed 713 cases of harmful online content, coming primarily from Facebook.

The research team relied on a combined approach using manual digital observation, keyword-based tracking, and reports received from impacted users. A dedicated platform was established to receive reports, integrated within the coalition’s website. 

The monitoring process revealed three major trends that have emerged in Iraq over this period. The first is an intensification of hate speech, incitement, and accusations of treason. Second, discourse around the war has shifted from treating it as an external event to wielding it as a tool for the mobilization of domestic actors across the whole political and social spectrum. The monitoring team concluded based on the content analysed, that Iraqi digital spaces no longer just follow regional events, they turn them inward, using them to fuel debates about domestic issues such as: who controls weapons, what role the United States plays, how much power armed groups should have, the future of political balances in Iraq, historical memory and religious themes. The third trend, identified by the organizations conducting the monitoring, point at mounting  evidence of networked coordination in digital campaigns such as repeated phrasing across different posts and accounts, synchronized timing in the released of content, and the recycling of clips, allegations, and hashtags. While these patterns stop short of proving centralized command, they point strongly to organized, or at minimum semi-organized, influence operations.

In response to these worrying trends, several recommendations have been brought forward by the organizations of the coalition. First, given the scale and the speed of escalation observed, there is a need to move toward a more responsive and real-time monitoring model. The data clearly shows an increase in the targeting of journalists, analysts, and content creators, requiring rapid and practical protection mechanisms. Given the rise of disinformation and AI-generated content, verification capacity must be scaled and decentralized. The findings also confirm that harmful content is amplified not only by producers but also by audience behaviour and emotional engagement, pointing to the critical need to step up in Media and Information Literacy training efforts. Lastly, the dataset confirms that women face disproportionate and targeted digital violence, requiring focused intervention addressing Technology Facilitated Gender Based Violence.

UNESCO will continue supporting local actors in addressing these challenges through expanded capacity-building initiatives on Media and Information Literacy (MIL), safety training for content creators and journalists, and stronger support to enhance fact-checking capacities. These activities are part of the Social Media 4 Peace project, which has been implemented in Iraq since 2025.

One of SM4P’s core objectives is to strengthen the capacity of local actors to collectively address the challenges of harmful online content through evidence-based methods grounded in human rights principles. In Iraq, SM4P has brought together a coalition of local organizations and is supporting them in advancing a rights-based approach to digital platform governance.

This coalition-based approach is particularly valuable, as local partners bring deep understanding of cultural nuances, political contexts, and community dynamics. Iraq joins similar initiatives supported by SM4P in Indonesia, Kenya, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Colombia, South Africa, and Kyrgyzstan. This work is funded by the European Union, who is a key partner of UNESCO in advancing rights-based governance of digital platforms with a multistakeholder approach.
